model.name: Form / Submission
model.purpose: Model the paired instrument definition and the completed, validated, transmitted response package so an agent can define a form, capture and constrain answers, submit them, and operate the resulting acceptance/rejection lifecycle with defensible provenance.
model.scope_statement: Covers (a) the form/instrument definition: identity, versioning, publication state, item tree, answer value domains, conditional logic and mandated respondent notices; and (b) the submission instance: answer payload, attachments, validation runs, status lifecycle, adjudication, attestation, audit trail, disposition and downstream extraction. Every authoritative source pairs the two (FHIR Questionnaire<->QuestionnaireResponse via linkId; XForms model/bind<->instance/submission; CDISC FormDef<->FormData; HTML form element<->entry list; ECF filing profile<->FilingMessage), and the binding contract only exists across the pair, so splitting them would orphan the contract. Format-neutral: JSON, XML, multipart, Markdown, Git, MCP and MongoDB are projections.
in_scope: Instrument definition: canonical identity, version lineage, publication state, effectivity, issuing authority
Item tree: stable link identifiers, item types, ordering, nesting, repeats, required flags
Answer value domains: datatypes, governed code lists, ranges, patterns, units, answer-constraint modes
Conditional enablement, calculated/derived items and relevance-driven pruning
Mandated respondent notices: legal authority, obligation, purpose, routine uses, control number and expiry, burden statement
Submission instance identity and immutable binding to an exact instrument version
Answer payload composition, repeats, ordering and missingness semantics
Attachments and supporting evidence carried in or referenced by the package
Constraint validation, validity states, validation tiers and authoritative revalidation on receipt
Submission status model, permitted transitions and enforced step sequencing
Review/adjudication outcomes, reason codes, amendment, withdrawal and resubmission
Respondent/author/submitter roles, delegation and attestation with signature manifestation
Time-stamped audit trail, reason for change, and the separation of event time from ingestion time
Access control, field-level sensitivity, redaction and public release
Retention, disposition, legal hold and erasure reconciliation
Serialization profiles, canonical form for digesting, and downstream extraction mapping
Acknowledgement/receipt, channel semantics and duplicate detection
Accessible error communication, error prevention and respondent-burden quality metrics
out_of_scope: The generic records programme (registration, classification scheme, disposal authority as an instrument of governance) - belongs to WM-REC-001 Record
Party/Agent identity as an entity (natural person, organisation, credential) - referenced only
Binary document/file object modelling, format migration and rendition management - referenced only
Cryptographic signature construction and trust-service levels (certificate chains, seal validation) - aligned, not restated
Case, matter or business-process orchestration beyond the submission's own status
Payment, fee assessment and financial transaction handling
Consent as a standalone legal instrument with its own lifecycle
Survey methodology and statistical estimation (sampling frames, weighting, imputation)
Message transport infrastructure, queuing and notification delivery guarantees
User interface rendering, layout and theming

boundary_notes.distinction: Record governs registration, classification and disposal of any record. Form/Submission governs the pre-record surface: the instrument that elicits data, the validation and adjudication that decide whether a package becomes a record, and the answer<->question binding that Record does not carry. An accepted submission is declared into the Record model; a rejected or abandoned draft usually never becomes one.

boundary_notes.neighbor: Observation / semantic clinical or business record
boundary_notes.distinction: QuestionnaireResponse deliberately preserves the specific phrasing and organisation of the questions; Observation preserves only the semantic meaning. Form/Submission is the wording-faithful artifact; extracted semantic records are separate downstream entities linked by item.definition.

This model records the signature manifestation and its binding to the payload (printed name, date and time, meaning of the signature, non-transferability). It does not model certificate chains, trust lists or validation algorithms.

The model carries part-level metadata (field name, filename, media type, charset, role as lead vs connected document, digest, or a reference URI) but not the document's own lifecycle, renditions or format policy.

The submission has its own status and transitions. Downstream docketing, case assignment and business processing are separate; ECF separates filing review status from docketing status precisely because the two can disagree.
Items bind to governed answer value sets by reference. Curation, versioning and publication of those code lists is out of scope.

boundary_notes.neighbor: Instrument definition vs submission instance (internal boundary, review-required)
boundary_notes.distinction: Some registries split these into two entries. This model keeps them together because the linkId/definition binding contract, version pinning and validation semantics span both and would be orphaned by a split. If the registry later splits them, the split line is: everything under bundle 'instrument-definition' moves out and bundles 2-7 stay, with the version-binding finding duplicated as a REFERENCE.

bundles.name: Instrument definition
bundles.description: The governed form definition: what is asked, how it is identified and versioned, what answers are permitted, what logic applies, and what notices it must carry.
bundles.rationale: Every authoritative pairing (FHIR Questionnaire, XForms model/bind, CDISC FormDef, HTML form element) treats the definition as a separately identified and versioned artifact that responses bind to. Without it the answer payload is uninterpretable.

layers.name: Instrument identity and publication
layers.description: How a form definition is named, versioned and moved through publication states so a submission can pin an exact, immutable definition.

findings.name: Instrument identity, version lineage and publication state
findings.description: The instrument carries a canonical identifier plus business identifiers, an ordered version string with a declared ordering algorithm, a publication status, an experimental flag, an effective period and approval/review dates. Submissions bind to a specific version, so version identity is a correctness requirement, not metadata hygiene.

questions.text: Which identifier is authoritative for this form definition: the issuing authority's official form number, a governed canonical URI, or a locally minted UUID?
answer_data: official form number or control number
locally assigned UUID/ULID and its minting authority

questions.text: How is a substantive new version distinguished from an editorial correction, and which algorithm orders versions?
answer_data: version ordering algorithm (semver, natural, integer, custom)

questions.text: In which publication state is the instrument, and during exactly which period may it accept new submissions?
Which authority owns the instrument and may approve or retire a version?

data_elements.name: Instrument canonical URI
data_elements.description: Globally governed identifier for the instrument independent of any storage location.

data_elements.name: Instrument business identifier
data_elements.description: Identifier assigned by the issuing authority, such as an official form number or an OMB control number.

data_elements.name: Instrument version
data_elements.description: Version label for this definition, ordered by a declared version algorithm.

data_elements.name: Instrument publication status
data_elements.description: Coded publication state governing whether the instrument may be used.

data_elements.name: Instrument effective period
data_elements.description: Period during which the instrument version is valid for new submissions.

artifacts.name: Instrument version manifest
artifacts.description: The immutable published definition of one instrument version, including its identity, item tree, constraints and notices, addressable by canonical URI plus version.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Canonical URI plus version string; where an issuing authority assigns a form/control number, that number is the authoritative business identifier and the URI is the resolvable alias.

layers.name: Item model and answer constraints
layers.description: The ordered item tree, the stable link identifiers that bind responses to questions, the permitted value domains, and the conditional and derived logic.

findings.name: Item tree and link identifier contract
findings.description: Items form an ordered, nestable tree of groups, display elements and answerable questions. Each item carries a link identifier that is the sole contract between definition and response; FHIR makes item.linkId mandatory on every response item and requires the response structure to stay consistent with the definition's grouping and nesting.

questions.text: Is each item's link identifier unique within the instrument and immutable across the version lineage, and is reuse for a different question forbidden?
How are groups, repeating groups and display-only items distinguished from answerable questions?
Must the response tree mirror the definition tree exactly, including nesting and sibling order?
Is the presentation and transmission order of items semantically significant for interpretation or for legal completeness?

data_elements.name: Item link identifier
data_elements.description: Stable identifier for one item, used identically in the definition and in every response.

data_elements.name: Item type
data_elements.description: Coded kind of item (group, display, boolean, decimal, integer, date, dateTime, string, choice, attachment and so on).

data_elements.name: Parent item link identifier
data_elements.description: Reference to the enclosing group item, expressing tree position.

data_elements.name: Item repeats flag
data_elements.description: Whether the item or group may occur more than once in a response.

data_elements.name: Item required flag
data_elements.description: Whether an answer must be present for the response to be considered complete.

artifacts.name: Item outline / instrument map
artifacts.description: Flattened, ordered listing of every item with link identifier, type, parent, repeats and required flags, used to validate response structure and to drive rendering and extraction.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Derived artifact identified by instrument canonical URI plus version; not independently versioned.

findings.name: Answer datatypes and value domains
findings.description: Each answerable item declares a value type and a permitted value domain: a governed code list, an enumerated option set, numeric bounds, string length and pattern, or a unit-bearing quantity. Whether free text may accompany or replace coded options is itself a declared mode.

questions.text: Which datatype system defines the permitted value type for each item, and is it declared in the instrument or inherited from a schema?
Is the answer restricted to a governed value set, and may free text be supplied alongside or instead of a coded option?
answer_data: answer constraint mode (options only, options or type, options or string)

questions.text: For quantity answers, which unit of measure and which precision or significant figures are required?
Which value-domain rules are declared in the instrument versus enforced only by the receiving system, and is any format keyword treated as an assertion rather than an annotation?

data_elements.name: Answer value type
data_elements.description: Datatype permitted for the item's answer.

data_elements.name: Answer value set reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the governed code list that constrains permitted coded answers.

data_elements.name: Answer constraint mode
data_elements.description: Whether only listed options, options plus a typed value, or options plus free string are permitted.

data_elements.name: Answer bounds and length limits
data_elements.description: Numeric minimum/maximum, string maximum length and regular-expression pattern constraining the answer.

data_elements.name: Answer unit of measure
data_elements.description: Unit and unit system required for quantity answers.

artifacts.name: Value domain binding table
artifacts.description: Per-item record of the value type, bound value set and version, option list, bounds and unit, used to reproduce validation independently of any runtime.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by instrument version plus item link identifier; value set bindings carry their own resolved version.

findings.name: Conditional enablement and derived values
findings.description: Items may be enabled by conditions over other answers with a declared combination behaviour, may be read-only or computed, and may be irrelevant. XForms prunes irrelevant nodes at serialization, so relevance directly changes what is transmitted and therefore what is validated and retained.

questions.text: Under what conditions is each item enabled, and how are multiple conditions combined?
Are values for disabled or irrelevant items pruned from the transmitted payload, retained as explicit nulls, or retained with a coded reason?
answer_data: coded missingness value used for disabled items

questions.text: Which items are computed rather than entered, and is the computation re-evaluated authoritatively by the receiver at submission time?
How are dependency cycles among conditional and calculated items detected, and is a cyclic instrument rejected at publication?

data_elements.name: Enablement condition
data_elements.description: Condition over another item's answer that controls whether this item is enabled.

data_elements.name: Enablement combination behaviour
data_elements.description: Whether all or any conditions must hold for the item to be enabled.

data_elements.name: Calculation expression
data_elements.description: Expression producing a derived answer value for a computed item.

data_elements.name: Relevance pruning policy
data_elements.description: Declared rule for whether irrelevant nodes are removed before serialization.

artifacts.name: Skip-logic dependency graph
artifacts.description: Resolved graph of enablement and calculation dependencies among items, used to prove acyclicity and to reproduce which items were in scope for a given response.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Derived from and identified by the instrument version it was computed from.

layers.name: Mandated notices and respondent burden
layers.description: Disclosures the instrument itself must carry before it may lawfully collect, and the burden and utility justification behind the collection.

findings.name: Regulatory notice block and burden statement
findings.description: Where a collection is regulated, the instrument must display specified content on the form itself: the authorising authority, whether response is mandatory or voluntary, the principal purposes and routine uses, the effects of not responding, a currently valid control number with its expiration, and an estimated burden. These are properties of the instrument, and an expired control number invalidates the collection rather than merely the paperwork.

questions.text: Which statutory or delegated authority permits or compels this collection, and is response mandatory, voluntary, or required to obtain a benefit?
What control number and expiration date are displayed, and how are submissions received after expiry handled?
What are the stated principal purposes and routine uses of the collected data, and where are they published?
What per-respondent burden is estimated, how was it derived, and what evidence of practical utility supports the collection?

data_elements.name: Legal authority citation
data_elements.description: Citation of the authority under which the information is solicited.

data_elements.name: Response obligation
data_elements.description: Whether a response is mandatory, voluntary or required to obtain or retain a benefit.

data_elements.name: Collection control number
data_elements.description: Currently valid control number that must be displayed on the collection instrument.

data_elements.name: Control number expiration date
data_elements.description: Date after which the displayed control number is no longer valid.

data_elements.name: Estimated respondent burden
data_elements.description: Estimated time, effort or cost per response.

artifacts.name: Notice and disclosure block
artifacts.description: The exact rendered notice text carried on or with the instrument, retained as issued so that what a respondent was actually shown can be reproduced years later.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by instrument version plus notice revision; retained verbatim rather than regenerated.

bundles.name: Submission instance
bundles.description: The concrete response package: its identity, its immutable binding to an instrument version, its answer set and its attachments.
bundles.rationale: FHIR generates a distinct response per subject per occasion and requires a 1..1 canonical binding to the questionnaire; ECF treats the filing as a package of lead and connected documents. The instance is a first-class thing with its own identity, not a view over the definition.

layers.name: Submission identity and instrument binding
layers.description: How a submission is identified across parties and how it pins the exact definition it answers.

findings.name: Submission identity and instrument version binding
findings.description: A submission carries the receiving authority's identifier, the submitter's own reference and, where neither exists, a locally minted UUID/ULID. It binds to exactly one instrument version; FHIR makes that canonical reference mandatory. Drafts created against a version that is later superseded are the sharp edge: the binding must either be pinned or explicitly migrated with a recorded decision.

questions.text: Which identifier is authoritative for this submission: the receiving authority's receipt or filing number, the submitter's own reference, or an internally minted UUID?
To exactly which instrument version is this submission bound, and is that binding immutable once the submission leaves draft?
What happens to an in-progress draft when the bound instrument version is superseded or retired?
What is this submission about, and which prior request, order or submission is it based on or part of?

data_elements.name: Submission identifier
data_elements.description: Authoritative identifier for the submission instance.

data_elements.name: Submitter's own reference
data_elements.description: Identifier assigned by the submitting party for its own tracking.

data_elements.name: Bound instrument version reference
data_elements.description: Canonical reference to the exact instrument version this submission answers.

data_elements.name: Submission subject
data_elements.description: The person, organisation or thing the answers are about, where distinct from the respondent.

data_elements.name: Based-on / part-of reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the request, plan or larger package this submission fulfils or belongs to.

artifacts.name: Submission package header
artifacts.description: The identifying envelope of the package: identifiers, bound instrument version, subject, sender and receiver, and package composition, separable from the answer payload for routing and audit.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Receiving-authority identifier first; submitter reference retained as a cross-reference; UUID/ULID only when neither is available.

layers.name: Answer payload and attachments
layers.description: The answer set with its repetition, ordering and missingness semantics, plus attached supporting evidence.

findings.name: Answer set composition and missingness semantics
findings.description: An item may carry several answers and groups may repeat, so the payload is a tree, not a map. RFC 7578 forbids coalescing identically named parts and asks that ordering be preserved. The hardest distinction is missingness: not asked, disabled by logic, asked and left blank, not applicable, and declined are five different facts that a single absent key cannot express.

questions.text: How are multiple answers to one item and repeated groups represented so that duplicates are not collapsed and occurrence identity is preserved?
How is not asked distinguished from disabled by logic, left blank, not applicable and declined to answer?
answer_data: absent vs null vs empty-string convention

questions.text: Is the transmitted order of answer entries semantically significant, and must it be preserved through every projection?
Is a partial payload a valid instance, and which items may be absent while the package remains well-formed?

data_elements.name: Answer entry
data_elements.description: One recorded answer bound to an item link identifier, with its value and occurrence position.

data_elements.name: Answer value
data_elements.description: The typed value supplied for an item, whose datatype is governed by the bound instrument item.

data_elements.name: Answer occurrence index
data_elements.description: Ordinal distinguishing repeated answers or repeated group instances.

data_elements.name: Missingness reason
data_elements.description: Coded explanation for the absence of an answer.

artifacts.name: Answer payload
artifacts.description: The complete answer tree as submitted, retained in canonical form so it can be revalidated, digested and signed independently of the transport encoding used.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by submission identifier plus payload revision number; each revision is retained rather than overwritten.

findings.name: Attachment parts and supporting evidence
findings.description: Files accompanying the answers carry field name, filename, media type, character encoding and size. ECF distinguishes lead from connected documents and prefers a binary URI reference over inline base64; RFC 7578 requires receivers to validate filenames against traversal attacks.

questions.text: Which attached document is the lead document and which are connected or supporting, and does that role affect adjudication?
What filename, media type, character encoding and size limits apply, and how are unsafe or ambiguous filenames neutralised on receipt?
Is the attachment carried inline in the package or referenced by URI, and which party guarantees its continued availability for the retention period?
What integrity value is recorded so the attachment can later be proven unaltered and reproduced as an accurate and complete copy?

data_elements.name: Attachment filename
data_elements.description: Original filename supplied by the sender, retained as sent and separately as sanitised.

data_elements.name: Attachment media type
data_elements.description: Declared media type of the attached part, with charset where textual.

data_elements.name: Attachment size
data_elements.description: Octet length of the attached content.

data_elements.name: Attachment role
data_elements.description: Whether the attachment is a lead document, a connected/supporting document or evidence for a specific item.

data_elements.name: Attachment digest
data_elements.description: Cryptographic digest and algorithm proving the attached content is unaltered.

artifacts.name: Attached document part
artifacts.description: One supporting file transmitted with or referenced by the submission, retained with its part metadata and digest.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Submission identifier plus part name plus sequence; the digest is the integrity identity and the filename is never treated as an identifier.

bundles.name: Validation and lifecycle
bundles.description: How a submission is checked, what states it may occupy, which transitions are permitted, and how acceptance, rejection and correction are decided and recorded.
bundles.rationale: The registry purpose names a validation lifecycle. HTML/XForms supply the declarative constraint layer, ECF supplies review and docketing statuses that can disagree, FHIR supplies the response status value set, and 21 CFR 11.10(f) supplies the normative requirement to enforce step sequencing.

layers.name: Constraint validation
layers.description: The declared constraint set, the validity states failures produce, and which party's verdict is authoritative.

findings.name: Constraint model and validity states
findings.description: Constraints are declared on items and produce specific validity states on failure (value missing, type mismatch, pattern mismatch, too long, too short, range underflow/overflow, step mismatch, bad input, custom error). Crucially, elements can be barred from constraint validation - disabled, read-only or irrelevant items never block submission - and a novalidate/validate=false path exists by design for saving incomplete work.

questions.text: Which constraint is declared on each item and which validity state does its failure produce?
Which items are barred from constraint validation because they are disabled, read-only or irrelevant, and therefore never block submission?
Is a declared format treated as a non-blocking annotation or as an enforced assertion, and who made that choice?
May validation be deliberately bypassed to save an incomplete draft, and under whose authority is the bypass recorded?

data_elements.name: Constraint identifier
data_elements.description: Stable identifier for one declared constraint or edit check.

data_elements.name: Constraint expression
data_elements.description: The declarative rule evaluated against the answer set.

data_elements.name: Validity state code
data_elements.description: Coded reason an answer fails its constraint.

data_elements.name: Validation bypass flag
data_elements.description: Whether validation was intentionally suppressed for this evaluation.

artifacts.name: Constraint / edit-check specification
artifacts.description: The full set of declared checks for an instrument version, retained so a historical validation verdict can be reproduced exactly.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Instrument canonical URI plus version plus rule-set revision.

findings.name: Validation tiers and authoritative revalidation
findings.description: Validation occurs at several tiers: declarative in-form checks, receiver structural revalidation, and business or eligibility rules applied later. Only one tier can be authoritative. 21 CFR 11.10(a) requires validated systems able to discern invalid or altered records, and ECF has the court validate on receipt before docketing - so the receiver, not the client, decides.

questions.text: When the sending and receiving systems disagree on validity, whose verdict is authoritative and how is the disagreement recorded?
Is the full constraint set re-evaluated on receipt, and against which instrument version - the bound one or the current one?
How is a validation outcome recorded so it can be replayed and audited after rule sets have changed?
What is the disposition of a payload that passes structural validation but fails a business or eligibility rule?

data_elements.name: Validation run identifier
data_elements.description: Identifier for one evaluation of a rule set against a payload revision.

data_elements.name: Validation tier
data_elements.description: Which tier performed the evaluation: in-form, receiver structural, or business rule.

data_elements.name: Validation outcome
data_elements.description: Coded overall result of the run.

data_elements.name: Validation issue
data_elements.description: One failure with its item reference, validity state, severity and message.

data_elements.name: Validation timestamp
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 instant at which the validation run completed.

artifacts.name: Validation report
artifacts.description: Immutable record of one validation run: rule set version, payload digest, outcome, issue list and timestamp, retained as the evidence behind an acceptance or rejection.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Submission identifier plus payload revision plus monotonic run sequence.

layers.name: Status model and transitions
layers.description: The states a submission may occupy and the rules and authority checks governing movement between them.

findings.name: Submission status model
findings.description: FHIR defines a required status value set (in-progress, completed, amended, entered-in-error, stopped) and marks status as a modifier element - status changes how the content may be interpreted, not merely how it is displayed. ECF tracks review status and docketing status separately, plus per-document statuses, precisely because a filing can be accepted for review yet fail to record.

questions.text: What is the current status of the submission, and is status a modifier that changes how the payload may lawfully be used?
Are review status and recording or docketing status tracked separately, and what does it mean when they disagree?
Is status tracked per item or per document as well as per submission, and does a part-level rejection reject the whole?
Which status values mean the content must not be used for clinical, legal, statistical or operational purposes?

data_elements.name: Submission status
data_elements.description: Coded current state of the submission as a whole.

data_elements.name: Review status
data_elements.description: Coded state of the receiving authority's review of the submission.

data_elements.name: Recording / docketing status
data_elements.description: Coded state of the submission's entry into the authoritative downstream record system.

data_elements.name: Part-level status
data_elements.description: Status of an individual document or item within the package.

artifacts.name: Status history
artifacts.description: Ordered, append-only record of every status the submission has held with actor, time and reason, used to answer what the status was at any past instant.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Submission identifier plus monotonic status sequence number.

findings.name: Transition rules and sequencing controls
findings.description: Not every status pair is a legal transition. 21 CFR 11.10(f) requires operational system checks that enforce permitted sequencing of steps and events, and 11.10(g) requires authority checks so only authorised individuals may perform an operation - together these make the transition table an enforced control, not documentation.

questions.text: Which status transitions are permitted, which are terminal, and what precondition guards each one?
What operational system check prevents steps from being performed out of order, for example signing before validation completes?
Which role is authorised to trigger each transition, and how is that authority checked at execution time?
May a submission in a terminal state be reopened, and what record must that create?

data_elements.name: Transition source status
data_elements.description: Status the submission held before the transition.

data_elements.name: Transition target status
data_elements.description: Status the submission holds after the transition.

data_elements.name: Transition precondition
data_elements.description: Condition that must hold for the transition to be permitted.

data_elements.name: Authorised role for transition
data_elements.description: Role permitted to execute the transition.

data_elements.name: Transition event time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 instant at which the transition occurred.

artifacts.name: State transition table
artifacts.description: Declared matrix of permitted transitions with guards and authorised roles, published per instrument or per collection programme so the enforced control can be inspected independently of code.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Owned by the collection programme; versioned independently of instrument versions and referenced by identifier plus version.

layers.name: Adjudication and remedy
layers.description: Human or automated decision on the submission, and the routes available to correct, replace or withdraw it.

findings.name: Decision outcome and reason codes
findings.description: An adjudication records who decided, under what authority, the coded outcome, a human-readable explanation and any remediation instruction. ECF returns an error code with zero meaning success and notifies review completion asynchronously. Whether acceptance backdates to original receipt is a substantive legal question, not a storage detail.

questions.text: Who reviewed the submission and under what delegated authority did they accept, reject or return it?
Which coded reason and human-readable explanation accompany a rejection or return, and are they drawn from a governed code list?
Can a submission be partly accepted, and what is the status and disposition of the unaccepted parts?
Does acceptance take effect from the original receipt time or from the decision time, and which governs any deadline?

data_elements.name: Decision outcome
data_elements.description: Coded adjudication result for the submission or a part of it.

data_elements.name: Decision reason code
data_elements.description: Governed code explaining the outcome, especially for rejection or return.

data_elements.name: Reviewer reference
data_elements.description: The individual or automated agent that made the decision.

data_elements.name: Decision time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 instant at which the decision was made.

data_elements.name: Effective filing time
data_elements.description: The time the submission is deemed to have been made for deadline purposes.

artifacts.name: Adjudication notice
artifacts.description: The decision communicated to the submitter, carrying outcome, reason codes, explanation, remediation instruction and effective time; retained as the authoritative statement of what the submitter was told.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Submission identifier plus monotonic decision sequence; supersession is expressed by reference, never by overwrite.

findings.name: Amendment, withdrawal and resubmission
findings.description: Corrections after submission are not edits. FHIR distinguishes amended from entered-in-error; CDISC requires an audit record with a reason for change on updates; 21 CFR 11 requires that changes not obscure previously recorded information. The choice between amending in place with version history and creating a superseding submission is a governance decision that must be declared.

questions.text: Is a correction recorded as a new version of the same submission or as a new submission that supersedes the prior one, and who decided that convention?
What explicitly links a resubmission to the rejected or withdrawn submission it replaces?
Is superseded or entered-in-error content retained and retrievable, and how is it excluded from downstream use without being destroyed?
Who may withdraw a submission and up to which point in the lifecycle?

data_elements.name: Amendment-of reference
data_elements.description: Reference from a corrected version to the version it amends.

data_elements.name: Supersedes / superseded-by reference
data_elements.description: Bidirectional link between a replacing submission and the one it replaces.

data_elements.name: Correction type
data_elements.description: Whether the change is an amendment, an entered-in-error retraction, a withdrawal or a resubmission after rejection.

data_elements.name: Reason for change
data_elements.description: Recorded justification for the correction, mandatory where regulated.

artifacts.name: Amendment / retraction record
artifacts.description: Record of one correction event: type, reason, affected items, actor, time and the links to prior and successor versions.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Submission identifier plus monotonic amendment sequence; never overwrites the amended payload revision.

bundles.name: Provenance, authority and attestation
bundles.description: Who supplied, recorded, signed and transmitted the submission, under what authority, and the time-stamped trail that proves it.
bundles.rationale: FHIR separates subject, author and source as distinct elements; CDISC records user, location, timestamp and reason for change; 21 CFR 11.50 and 11.70 specify what a signature must manifest and how it must bind. Conflating these roles destroys the evidentiary value of the package.

layers.name: Actors, authority and attestation
layers.description: Role separation among respondent, recorder, submitter and subject, the basis for acting on another's behalf, and the signature that closes the package.

findings.name: Respondent, author and submitter roles
findings.description: FHIR keeps source (who answered), author (who recorded) and subject (who the answers are about) as three separate elements, and ECF adds a filer/sender distinct from all three. Assisted or proxy completion, interviewer-administered forms and agent-filed packages all produce different combinations, and the difference is legally material.

questions.text: Who supplied the answers, who recorded them and who transmitted the package, and are any of these the same party?
Is the submission made on behalf of another party, and what evidence establishes that representation?
answer_data: representation basis (power of attorney, licence, delegation record)

questions.text: At which site, organisational unit or jurisdiction was the data captured, and does that affect which rules apply?
What identity proofing or authentication was performed on the submitter before the package was accepted?

data_elements.name: Respondent / source reference
data_elements.description: The party who supplied the answers.

data_elements.name: Author / recorder reference
data_elements.description: The party who entered or transcribed the answers.

data_elements.name: Submitter reference
data_elements.description: The party that transmitted the package to the receiving authority.

data_elements.name: On-behalf-of reference
data_elements.description: The party the submitter represents, where different from the submitter.

data_elements.name: Capture location reference
data_elements.description: Site or organisational location where the answers were captured.

artifacts.name: Role assignment and representation record
artifacts.description: Record binding each party to its role on this submission, with the evidence supporting any representation or delegation.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Keyed by submission identifier plus role code plus party reference.

findings.name: Declaration and signature manifestation
findings.description: 21 CFR 11.50 requires a signed record to carry the printed name of the signer, the date and time of signing, and the meaning of the signature (review, approval, responsibility, authorship); 11.70 requires the signature be linked so it cannot be excised, copied or transferred. The declaration text the signer accepted must be retained verbatim, not regenerated from a current template.

questions.text: What exact declaration or certification text did the signer accept, and what meaning is attached to the signature?
By what method was the record signed, and how is the signature bound to this exact payload so it cannot be excised or transferred to another record?
What identity assurance and authority check were performed before the signature was accepted?
Is the signature manifestation reproducible in human-readable form on any export or printed copy?

data_elements.name: Printed name of signer
data_elements.description: Human-readable name of the signer as it must appear on the signed record.

data_elements.name: Signature execution time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 instant at which the signature was executed.

data_elements.name: Meaning of signature
data_elements.description: Coded meaning such as review, approval, responsibility or authorship.

data_elements.name: Signed payload digest
data_elements.description: Digest of the canonical payload the signature covers.

data_elements.name: Declaration text as presented
data_elements.description: Verbatim certification or attestation text shown to the signer.

artifacts.name: Signature block
artifacts.description: The signature and its manifestation bound to the canonical payload digest, retained with the declaration text so the act of signing can be reconstructed and defended.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Submission identifier plus payload revision plus signer plus signature sequence; the payload digest is the binding key.

layers.name: Audit trail and temporal record
layers.description: The independent, time-stamped record of every action on the submission, and the distinct time points that govern deadlines and timeliness.

findings.name: Audit record and reason for change
findings.description: 21 CFR 11.10(e) requires secure, computer-generated, time-stamped audit trails that independently record the date and time of operator entries and actions that create, modify or delete records, without obscuring prior values. CDISC pairs each change with user, location, timestamp, reason for change and source identifier, plus a transaction type distinguishing insert from update and removal.

questions.text: What audit entry is generated for each create, modify and delete action on the submission, and does it capture the prior value?
For which classes of change is a reason for change mandatory, and is a free-text reason acceptable or must it be coded?
Is the audit trail generated independently of the operator and protected from modification or deletion by the parties it records?
For how long is the audit trail retained relative to the submission itself, and is it disposed of together with the record?

data_elements.name: Audit entry identifier
data_elements.description: Identifier of one immutable audit entry.

data_elements.name: Audit action
data_elements.description: Coded action recorded: create, read, update, delete, sign, transmit, decide, export or dispose.

data_elements.name: Audit actor reference
data_elements.description: The individual or system agent that performed the action.

data_elements.name: Audit timestamp
data_elements.description: System-generated RFC 3339 instant of the action, independent of operator-supplied times.

data_elements.name: Reason for change
data_elements.description: Recorded justification accompanying a modification or deletion.

data_elements.name: Transaction type
data_elements.description: Whether the entry represents an insert, update, removal or upsert of data.

artifacts.name: Audit trail log
artifacts.description: Append-only, tamper-evident sequence of audit entries for the submission, retrievable and exportable as an accurate and complete copy for inspection.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Submission identifier plus monotonic audit sequence; entries are never renumbered or reordered.

findings.name: Temporal model, deadlines and timeliness
findings.description: A submission has many distinct times: started, last saved, authored, signed, transmitted, received, decided and disposed. RFC 3339 requires an explicit offset or Z on each, and reserves -00:00 for a known UTC instant with unknown local offset. Deadlines are evaluated in the receiving authority's timezone, which is frequently not the respondent's - and ECF requires submission date and time as filing metadata precisely because that instant has legal effect.

questions.text: Which distinct time points are recorded for this submission: started, last saved, authored, signed, transmitted, received, decided and disposed?
How is event time (when the respondent answered or signed) kept separate from observation or ingestion time (when the receiver recorded it), and which is used for reporting?
In which timezone is a deadline evaluated, and is an explicit offset recorded with every stored timestamp?
If a submission is rejected and corrected within a grace period, which time counts for deadline compliance?
How long may a draft remain untouched before it expires, and is the respondent warned before expiry?

data_elements.name: Authored time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 instant when the answers were gathered or authored by the respondent.

data_elements.name: Received time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 instant at which the receiving authority took delivery of the package.

data_elements.name: Deadline instant
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 instant by which the submission must be received, with the governing offset.

data_elements.name: Draft expiry duration
data_elements.description: Period of inactivity after which an unsubmitted draft expires.

findings.inline_only_rationale: These are timestamp attributes carried on the submission header, status history, audit trail and decision notice rather than a separate retained object. Materialising a standalone time artifact would duplicate the audit trail log and create a second, divergent source of truth for legally operative instants.

bundles.name: Governance, privacy and disposition
bundles.description: Who may see the submission and which parts, what is published or redacted, and how the package is ultimately retained, transferred or destroyed.
bundles.rationale: The Privacy Act constrains what may be collected and disclosed and requires accuracy and relevance; 21 CFR 11.10(c) and (g) require retrievability through the retention period and authority checks; NARA's Universal ERM Requirements structure capture, maintenance, disposal and transfer. These obligations attach to the submission before it is declared a record.

layers.name: Access, confidentiality and disclosure
layers.description: Authorisation to read and act on a submission, sensitivity at item level, and controlled release to third parties or the public.

findings.name: Access control and field-level sensitivity
findings.description: Authority checks must ensure only authorised individuals can use the system, sign, access the operation or alter a record. Submissions are rarely uniformly sensitive: a single package can mix routine fields with identifiers, health data or protected identities, so authorisation granularity below the package is normal rather than exceptional.

questions.text: Which roles may read, amend, decide on or export the submission, and at what granularity is that authorisation expressed?
Which items carry heightened sensitivity requiring separate authorisation or separate storage?
Is any part of the submission sealed or restricted from the submitting or responding parties themselves?
How is each access to and export of a submission logged, and are denied attempts recorded too?

data_elements.name: Access policy reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the authorisation policy governing this submission.

data_elements.name: Confidentiality classification
data_elements.description: Coded confidentiality level of the submission or of a part.

data_elements.name: Sensitive item link identifiers
data_elements.description: Items requiring elevated authorisation or separate handling.

data_elements.name: Access log entry
data_elements.description: Record of one read, export or disclosure with actor, purpose and time.

artifacts.name: Access policy binding
artifacts.description: The concrete grant set attached to this submission or instrument, resolvable to roles, scopes, item-level exceptions and effective periods.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Keyed by submission or instrument identifier plus policy identifier plus policy version.

findings.name: Redaction and public release
findings.description: Some submissions are published - court filings, public comments, regulatory disclosures. Release produces a distinct derived artifact with its own identifier, its own integrity value and a recorded authorisation, and the redaction rule set applied must be retained so the release can be audited against what was actually withheld.

questions.text: Is any version of this submission published or disclosed beyond the receiving authority, and to whom?
Which items or document regions must be redacted before release, and under which rule set?
answer_data: redaction rule set reference and version

questions.text: Who authorises release, and is the authorisation recorded separately from the release itself?
Is the redacted release a distinct artifact with its own identifier and integrity value, so it is never confused with the original?

data_elements.name: Publication status
data_elements.description: Whether and how the submission has been released beyond the receiving authority.

data_elements.name: Redaction rule set reference
data_elements.description: The versioned rule set applied to produce the released copy.

data_elements.name: Released copy identifier
data_elements.description: Identifier of the derived, redacted artifact released to a third party or the public.

data_elements.name: Release authorisation reference
data_elements.description: Party and record authorising the release.

artifacts.name: Redacted public copy
artifacts.description: Derived release artifact carrying its own identifier, digest, derivation link and applied rule set version.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Own identifier in a release namespace, plus a derivation reference to the source submission revision; never reuses the submission identifier.

layers.name: Retention and disposition
layers.description: How long the submission and its derivatives are kept, under whose authority they are destroyed or transferred, and how erasure requests are reconciled.

findings.name: Retention, disposition and erasure reconciliation
findings.description: Records must remain accurately and readily retrievable throughout the retention period, and disposal or transfer happens under a named authority. Drafts and abandoned answers are the neglected case - they contain personal data but often no disposition instruction. Erasure requests and statutory retention genuinely conflict, and the model must record the outcome of that conflict rather than resolve it silently.

questions.text: Which event starts the retention clock - receipt, final decision, or closure of the parent matter - and how long is the period?
Under which named disposition authority is the submission destroyed or transferred, and to which destination?
How are abandoned drafts and never-submitted answers disposed of differently from accepted submissions?
How is an erasure or correction request from the respondent reconciled with a statutory retention obligation, and is a refusal recorded?
answer_data: refusal reasons given to the requester

questions.text: Is a legal hold or preservation order in force that suspends the disposition schedule?

data_elements.name: Retention trigger event
data_elements.description: The event from which the retention period is calculated.

data_elements.name: Retention period
data_elements.description: Duration the submission and its audit trail must be kept.

data_elements.name: Disposition action
data_elements.description: Coded action to take at the end of retention: destroy, transfer or retain permanently.

data_elements.name: Disposition authority reference
data_elements.description: The approved schedule or authority permitting the disposition action.

data_elements.name: Legal hold flag
data_elements.description: Whether disposition is suspended by a hold or preservation obligation.

artifacts.name: Disposition instruction and certificate
artifacts.description: The binding instruction attached to the submission and, once executed, the certificate recording what was destroyed or transferred, by whom and when.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Submission identifier plus disposition event sequence, cross-referenced to the governing schedule identifier and version.

bundles.name: Interoperability and transport
bundles.description: How the submission is serialised, digested, mapped downstream, transmitted and acknowledged without semantic loss.
bundles.rationale: CDISC keeps one abstract model across XML and JSON serializations; XForms declares serialization separately from the model; RFC 7578 and HTML define wire encodings; FHIR item.definition carries the mapping to downstream elements. Format neutrality is only real if the canonical form is named explicitly.

layers.name: Serialization and downstream mapping
layers.description: The canonical abstract form, its wire projections, and the declared mapping from items to downstream data elements.

findings.name: Serialization profile and format neutrality
findings.description: The semantics live in the abstract answer tree; urlencoded pairs, multipart parts, XML and JSON are projections. This matters operationally because signatures and digests must cover a single named canonical form, and because flat name/value encodings cannot represent repeating nested groups without a declared convention.

questions.text: Which serialization is the canonical form for digesting and signing, as distinct from the transport encodings permitted on the wire?
What character encoding is asserted for text values, and how is it signalled when the transport cannot carry an explicit declaration?
How are hierarchical and repeating groups represented in a flat name/value encoding without loss of nesting or occurrence identity?
Which encodings are permitted for a given channel, and who decides when they diverge from the instrument's declared serialization?

data_elements.name: Canonical form identifier
data_elements.description: Named canonical serialization used for digesting and signing.

data_elements.name: Transport encoding
data_elements.description: Encoding actually used on the wire for this transmission.

data_elements.name: Payload character encoding
data_elements.description: Character encoding asserted for textual values in the payload.

data_elements.name: Canonical payload digest
data_elements.description: Digest computed over the canonical form, used for integrity and signature binding.

artifacts.name: Canonical payload serialization
artifacts.description: The byte-exact canonical rendering of the answer payload retained alongside the abstract tree, so digests and signatures remain verifiable after any storage migration.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Submission identifier plus payload revision plus canonicalisation profile version; the digest is the verification key.

findings.name: Definition binding and downstream extraction
findings.description: Items may carry a definition URI pointing at a target data element, enabling answers to be extracted into semantic records. The boundary must be explicit: FHIR keeps the question-faithful response distinct from derived observations, so extraction produces new entities and does not displace the submission as source of truth.

questions.text: To which target data element does each item map, and is the mapping declared in the instrument or maintained externally?
Once answers are extracted downstream, is the extracted record authoritative or does the submission remain the source of truth?
How is the exact question wording preserved when answers are extracted into semantically typed records that discard phrasing?
answer_data: link back to instrument version and link identifier
rendering of original wording in the derived record

questions.text: How are extraction failures surfaced without invalidating an otherwise accepted submission?

data_elements.name: Item definition URI
data_elements.description: Reference from an item to the formal definition of the data element it populates.

data_elements.name: Extraction target reference
data_elements.description: The downstream record or element populated from this item.

data_elements.name: Extraction status
data_elements.description: Coded outcome of an extraction run for this submission.

data_elements.name: Mapping version
data_elements.description: Version of the mapping applied, so a past extraction can be reproduced.

artifacts.name: Extraction mapping manifest
artifacts.description: Record of one extraction run: mapping version, item-to-target pairs, produced record references, failures and timestamp.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Submission identifier plus mapping version plus monotonic extraction run sequence.

layers.name: Channel, receipt and duplicate handling
layers.description: How the package travels, what acknowledgement the submitter receives, and how repeated deliveries are resolved.

findings.name: Submission channel and acknowledgement
findings.description: XForms names the endpoint, method and replace behaviour and raises distinct done and error events; ECF returns a synchronous message status with an error code where zero means success, and reports the review result asynchronously afterwards. Three failure classes must stay distinguishable: transport failure, structural rejection and business rejection.

questions.text: Through which channel and endpoint was the submission transmitted, and was acceptance acknowledged synchronously or asynchronously?
What does the acknowledgement contain that lets the submitter prove the package was received at a particular instant?
How are transport errors distinguished from structural rejections and from business rejections in the response?
What subsequent notification is owed to the submitter, and within what interval must it arrive?

data_elements.name: Submission endpoint reference
data_elements.description: Address to which the package was transmitted.

data_elements.name: Acknowledgement identifier
data_elements.description: Identifier of the receipt issued by the receiving authority.

data_elements.name: Acknowledgement time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 instant at which receipt was acknowledged.

data_elements.name: Transport or processing error code
data_elements.description: Coded error returned by the receiving service, distinguishing transport from processing failure.

artifacts.name: Acknowledgement / receipt
artifacts.description: The receiving authority's statement that a specific package digest arrived at a specific instant, retained by both parties as the primary evidence of timely submission.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Receiving-authority receipt identifier; cross-referenced to the submission identifier and the acknowledged payload digest.

findings.name: Duplicate detection and idempotency
findings.description: At-least-once delivery and impatient respondents both produce repeated transmissions. FHIR treats each completion for a different subject or time as a distinct response, and ECF carries sender/receiver identifiers with a submission date and time - together these give the keys for deciding sameness. Note that a normative idempotency-key mechanism is common practice rather than a requirement in the sources consulted.

questions.text: Which key determines that two received packages are the same submission rather than two legitimately distinct ones?
answer_data: key components (submitter, instrument version, subject, payload digest)

questions.text: Within what window is a repeated transmission treated as a retry rather than a new submission?
What is returned when a duplicate is detected - the original receipt, a conflict error, or a new receipt referencing the original?

data_elements.name: Idempotency / deduplication key
data_elements.description: Key used to recognise a repeated delivery of the same logical submission.

data_elements.name: Duplicate-of reference
data_elements.description: Reference from a detected duplicate to the submission it repeats.

data_elements.name: Duplicate detection window
data_elements.description: Period during which repeated deliveries are treated as retries.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Duplicate-resolution facts are control metadata on a single transport exchange and are recorded inside the acknowledgement receipt and the audit trail log. A separate retained artifact would fragment the receipt evidence that the submitter actually relies on, and the sources consulted define no independent duplicate-resolution record.

bundles.name: Respondent experience and quality
bundles.description: How errors are communicated and prevented for the person completing the form, and how the collection's real burden and quality are measured.
bundles.rationale: WCAG 2.2 makes error identification, labels, error suggestion, error prevention, redundant entry and status messages normative success criteria at specific conformance levels; 5 CFR 1320 makes burden estimation and practical utility conditions of the collection. Both are properties of the form/submission surface, not of a generic UI model.

layers.name: Accessibility and error communication
layers.description: Normative requirements on how a form labels its inputs, reports failures and prevents costly mistakes.

findings.name: Error identification and suggestion
findings.description: WCAG 2.2 requires at Level A that input errors be automatically detected, the item identified and the error described in text (3.3.1), and that labels or instructions be provided where input is required (3.3.2); at Level AA it requires correction suggestions where known (3.3.3) and that status messages be programmatically determinable without receiving focus (4.1.3). These bind the shape of the validation issue objects, not just the styling.

questions.text: For each failed constraint, is the erroneous item identified and the error described in text rather than by colour or position alone?
Is a correction suggestion provided when one is known, and is it deliberately withheld where suggesting it would compromise security or purpose?
Are validation results and progress exposed programmatically so assistive technology is notified without moving focus?
Does every item requiring input carry a label or instruction, and do headings and labels describe topic or purpose?

data_elements.name: Error message text
data_elements.description: Human-readable description of one validation failure.

data_elements.name: Erroneous item reference
data_elements.description: Link identifier of the item the error concerns.

data_elements.name: Correction suggestion
data_elements.description: Suggested correction offered to the respondent where one is known.

data_elements.name: Item label or instruction
data_elements.description: Label or instruction presented with an item requiring input.

artifacts.name: Error message catalogue
artifacts.description: Governed set of message texts and suggestions keyed by constraint identifier and locale, retained per instrument version so the message a respondent actually saw can be reproduced.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Instrument version plus catalogue revision plus locale tag.

findings.name: Error prevention and confirmation
findings.description: WCAG 2.2 requires at Level AA that submissions with legal or financial consequences, or that modify user-controlled data, be reversible, checked, or confirmed (3.3.4), and at Level A that previously entered information not be redundantly re-requested (3.3.7). Whether a submission is legally binding therefore changes the mandatory interaction design, so the classification must be recorded on the instrument.

questions.text: Is this submission legally binding, financial, or a modification of user-controlled data, and therefore subject to the reversible, checked or confirmed requirement?
Is a review-and-confirm step presented before irreversible submission, and is the respondent's confirmation itself recorded?
Is information the respondent already supplied in the same process re-requested, and if so on what justification?
Is the purpose of each personal-data input programmatically identified so autofill and personalisation can operate?

data_elements.name: Consequence classification
data_elements.description: Whether the submission is legal, financial, data-modifying or routine, driving error-prevention obligations.

data_elements.name: Confirmation step present
data_elements.description: Whether a review-and-confirm step precedes irreversible submission.

data_elements.name: Prefilled item link identifiers
data_elements.description: Items populated from previously supplied information rather than re-requested.

data_elements.name: Input purpose token
data_elements.description: Programmatic purpose token for an input collecting information about the user.

artifacts.name: Confirmation summary presented to the respondent
artifacts.description: The exact review summary shown before final submission, retained so a later dispute about what the respondent confirmed can be resolved from evidence.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Submission identifier plus payload revision at the moment of confirmation; digest-linked to the payload it summarised.

layers.name: Quality and paradata
layers.description: Observed evidence about how the collection actually performs against its claimed burden and utility.

findings.name: Submission quality metrics and paradata
findings.description: Regulated collections must estimate burden and demonstrate practical utility that is actual rather than theoretical, and records must be accurate, relevant, timely and complete. Observed paradata - time to complete, abandonment point, item non-response, edit-check failure concentration and rejection rate - is the falsification test for those claims and the input to instrument revision.

questions.text: What measured time to complete is observed, and how does it compare with the published burden estimate?
What proportion of started submissions are abandoned, and at which item does abandonment concentrate?
Which items generate the most validation failures or rejections, and has the instrument been revised in response?
What evidence shows the collected data is actually used, and which items have never been consumed downstream?

data_elements.name: Measured completion duration
data_elements.description: Observed time from start to submission.

data_elements.name: Abandonment rate
data_elements.description: Proportion of started submissions never completed, with the concentrating item.

data_elements.name: Item non-response rate
data_elements.description: Proportion of submissions leaving a given item unanswered.

data_elements.name: Rejection rate
data_elements.description: Proportion of submissions rejected at review, by reason code.

artifacts.name: Quality and paradata report
artifacts.description: Periodic report on measured burden, abandonment, item non-response, failure concentration and downstream utilisation for one instrument version, feeding renewal and revision decisions.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Instrument version plus reporting period; periods do not overlap and are never restated in place.
